name: Antoine Ouilmette's house, the easternmost of the three houses west of the Kinzie house
aka: the easternmost no. 31 house on Whistler's draught (1808)
the cabin of Antoine Ouilmette, 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' (Currey 1912)
the house of Ouilmette, whose garden hid a soldier behind its currant bushes on 16 August 1812 (Wau-Bun)

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

documented_range.note: OPENS ON THE DRAUGHT'S DATE, CLOSES WITH THE DECADE THE EXCLUSION GIVES IT. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date in the parade of Whistler's draught, the first day a source draws this house; Ouilmette had lived at Chicago since 1790 by Currey's account and Mrs. Whistler counted his among the four huts of 1803 (Moses and Kirkland v1 p. 35), so it may well be older. It STANDS IN AUGUST 1812 BY THE SOURCES, not by continuity: Wau-Bun ch. XIX has Mrs. Helm hidden in it on the 16th and a sergeant climb in at its back window the next afternoon, and Currey (1912) has the family alone of the village's residents not leave their dwelling. Hubbard, listing every building in the present limits of Cook County when he came in 1818, still has 'a cabin on the north side occupied by Antoine Ouilmette' (his autobiography, the inventory of 1818). It closes on 31 December 1829, which is data/exclusions.json `ouilmette_cabin`'s own bound: Ouilmette left for Gross Pointe in the later 1820s and no source attests the cabin past that decade. Out of 1835. L-1812-ouilmette-2486.

change_note: Built T-2486 (2026-10-23). The third of the three houses Whistler draws across the river west of Kinzie's in January 1808, the one nearest Kinzie's, standing in the 1812 scene as Antoine Ouilmette's.

placement.position_note: SEATED BY STATED RULE, NOT MEASURED. Whistler draws three houses west of Kinzie's, each with a '31' ('Oather Dwelling Houses on opisite side River'), and says his outside distances are 'not laid down by a scale'. The north bank is opened out about the Kinzie house as built, by the drafter's own '52 yards in length' on the picket along this bank (2.497 times the drawing), as for La Lime's and Le Mai's houses. This is the smallest of the three and the one nearest Kinzie's, which is why it is Ouilmette's: Currey has his cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and 'a little in the rear of it', Wau-Bun 'close at hand'. The rule seats it a little behind the Kinzie house's line and 30 m west of it, which agrees with 'a little in the rear' and does not need to be moved to. tools/read_whistler_1808.py --check re-derives this seat from the sheet box and refuses it wet or on a neighbour. L-1812-ouilmette-2486.
placement.symbolic_location: The north bank of the main river WEST of the Kinzie house, the draught's east no. 31 house, between the middle one (La Lime's) and the building numbered 32 (the horse mill); fort-frame box E -117.0..-98.4 ft, N +406.5..+417.6 ft by the north-bank rule (data/traces/whistler_1808_fort_dearborn.json north_bank), facing south to the river. Its front stands about 2 m north of the line of the Kinzie house's back wall and 30 m west of it. This record's origin is the footprint's north-east corner, local E +1122.0, N +348.3, which a south facing puts at the frame's (0, 0).

footprint.note: 18.6 x 11.1 ft: the drawn box (42 x 25 px) at the index's forty feet to the inch, the scale every outside building is read at. The drawing is a small pictorial elevation, roof and front together, so the depth is an upper bound. The smallest of the three no. 31 houses, as Currey's 'less pretentious cabin' has it. L-1812-ouilmette-2486.

stories.note: The draught draws one storey of logs under the eaves, with no upper light.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About seven feet of log to the plate, a little under its neighbours' eight, for the smallest house on the bank; the draught gives no height.

construction.note: The draught draws the house in logs, the log ends standing out at both corners, as it draws the Kinzie house and the other two no. 31 houses. Hewn or round is not read off a drawing this small.

roof_type.note: The draught draws a pitched roof running along the front with its gables at the ends.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested; the neighbours' pitch. The draught's elevation is too small and too freely drawn to measure one from.

chimneys.note: The draught draws one chimney, standing against the house's west gable (sheet x 1124-1132).

chimney_end.note: The west gable, as the draught draws it. A south facing turns the footprint's +x to the west, so the stack stands at the ridge axis's max end.

front_set_out.note: THE DRAUGHT'S 'ONE LIGHT AND A DOOR', IN ITS ORDER. Read at T-2486 on a 12x gridded crop of the pinned sheet: from the river the door stands left of the middle (centre at 0.345 of the drawn box from its west end) and the one light right of it (0.607). Measured from the core's -x corner, the east end, that is the light at 2.23 m and the door at 3.71 m. Their sizes are the archetype's.

function.note: Whistler letters the three no. 31 houses 'Oather Dwelling Houses'; Currey calls Ouilmette's 'the less pretentious cabin of Antoine Ouilmette'.

occupants.value: Antoine Ouilmette's household: Ouilmette, a French Canadian at Chicago since 1790; his wife, a Potawatomi woman; their family; and in August 1812 his wife's sister, Mrs. Bisson. A Métis household.
occupants.note: WHO LIVED IN OUILMETTE'S HOUSE IS THE SOURCES'; WHICH DRAWN HOUSE WAS HIS IS INFERRED. Currey (1912, ch. II): 'Ouilmette was a Frenchman with an Indian wife, and had lived here since 1790. His wife, being a member of the Potawatami tribe, was awarded ... a tract of land on the north shore', the Wilmette Reservation; and in the August chapter, 'A sister of his wife, known in the accounts as Mrs. Bisson, was a member of this same household.' Wau-Bun ch. XIX describes both women as of mixed descent. Victoire Porthier, born Mirandeau, remembered that 'some of us lived in the Ouilmette house across the river from the fort' before the fort burned (Moses and Kirkland v1, lines 6776-6779 of the committed text). The house is the no. 31 house nearest Kinzie's because Currey puts Ouilmette's cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Wau-Bun 'close at hand' (T-2504's assignment, L-1812-lalime-lemai-2504).

citations.citation: Currey, J. Seymour. The Story of Old Fort Dearborn. Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912.
what_it_supplies: the house's builder, Jean Baptiste Point de Saible, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', and that he built it 'some time before 1779' near the present foot of Pine Street
its sale in 1797 to Le Mai, and Le Mai's sale to John Kinzie in 1804, Kinzie arriving 'in the fall of that year'
Kinzie's work on it: 'he repaired it, added a veranda, and planted four Lombardy poplars at the foot of the slope on which the house stood'
its orientation: 'The house faced toward the south, having the river directly in front and the lake a short distance to the east'
that it 'escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre' and 'was finally demolished in the early thirties'
Ouilmette's cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Pettell's 'small cabin near the Kinzie house'

the lake shore south of the river mouth before 1812, in the same chapter: 'mostly devoid of trees, a scanty growth of cottonwoods and pines, however, maintaining a precarious existence among the sand-dunes', the low sand-hills 'the predominant feature of the landscape' a mile or two south of the mouth (used by T-2768 for the pines on the south sand hills)
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension of the house, the piazza or the green
the number of the house's rooms, windows or chimneys
a date for the veranda or the poplars more exact than 'after the house came into the possession of John Kinzie'
the Sarony lithograph itself: the Gutenberg file carries only its caption, so the plate is not read here

citations.citation: Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, Pa-pa-ma-ta-be, "The Swift Walker", with an Introduction by Caroline M. McIlvaine, Librarian of the Chicago Historical Society (Chicago: R. R. Donnelley & Sons Company, The Lakeside Press, Christmas 1911) — The Lakeside Classics. Read in full for its Chicago material before 1836: the front matter, McIlvaine's Introduction (pages ix-xxvii), and Hubbard's own narrative at pages 27-41, 135-138, 141-144, 153-159, 165-174 and 178-182. Hubbard's letter of 25 July 1827, printed as a note at page 174, is a separate source record.

transcribes.work: Hubbard's own autobiographical narrative — his engagement with the American Fur Company at Montreal and Mackinaw, the voyage of September 1818, his first entry into Chicago on 1 October 1818, the fort and its neighbours as he first saw them, the Chicago portage and Mud Lake, Hubbard's Trail, the trading posts of the Illinois River, and the Winnebago Scare of 1827 — ending abruptly at November 1830
transcribes.date: Written in the 1880s; printed 1888 and again 1911. Describes 1818-1830.
transcribes.note: A participant's recollection at more than fifty years' distance, and the rung most of this reading sits on. It is a recollection and not a record: the Fort Dearborn measurements are paces remembered, the payment of page 167 is dated to the wrong year, and the commanders' list is Hubbard's own search of the War Department records, which he says failed for the years after June 1833. The Winnebago Scare section (pages 166-174) is footnoted as coming not from the Diary but 'from statements by Mr. Hubbard in Chicago Historical Series, No. 10', which is one remove further.

transcribes.work: Caroline M. McIlvaine's Introduction, pages ix-xxvii — a 1911 review of the fifty-six years the Autobiography does not cover, compiled from letters, memoranda, contemporaries' reminiscences and printed history, and quoting E. O. Gale's Reminiscences of Early Chicago, The Chicago American of 10 October 1835, the Sunday Times of 24 October 1875 and Henry E. Hamilton's 1907 biographical sketch
transcribes.note: EVERY STATEMENT THIS PROJECT TAKES ABOUT 1834, 1835 OR 1836 COMES FROM HERE AND NOT FROM HUBBARD. The brick building at La Salle and South Water, the five or six hundred inhabitants, the brig Illinois of 25 May 1835, the Green Tree Tavern, the fire engine, the Russell & Mather purchase, the canal commissioners and the water-works are all McIlvaine's, written seventy-six years after the scene, and several are quotations at a further remove. A run reaching for 'Hubbard on 1835' is reaching for McIlvaine.

transcribes.work: Editorial notes by Henry E. Hamilton, signed H. E. H., inserted in square brackets in the narrative — including the note at page 178 that the hog-driving of 1829-30 'was the beginning of the packing industry in Chicago' — and the publishers' preface and closing note
transcribes.date: 1888 (the notes); 1911 (the preface and the closing note, the latter signed C. M. M.)
transcribes.note: Compiler's judgements, sixty years after the events, printed inside the narrative's own type. bk_hub_101 and bk_hub_104 are read from this layer and say so.

what_it_supplies: Fort Dearborn's occupation chronology, dated to the day, from its establishment in 1804 to its final abandonment on 29 December 1836 — which puts the scene year inside a continuous garrison running from 1 October 1832

a full description of the second fort as a man who lived beside it in 1818 remembered it: fourteen-foot oak pickets, a block house at the south-west corner and a bastion at the north-west, whitewashed stockade and buildings, the officers' quarters outside the pickets with a piazza at second-storey level, the soldiers' quarters, the sutler's store in the north-east corner, two gates, two ten-foot guardhouses, a two-storey commissary storehouse and a brick magazine

the fort's surroundings: a four-acre garden, a military barn, a field running half a mile south, the ONE road, a fence line closed from river to river, the well by the south gate, and wash-houses on the sandy beach east of the pickets

the Factor House — two storeys, squared logs, a split-picket fence, Jouett to about 1810 and then John Dean — and the American Fur Company's round-log storehouse built by John Craft and occupied after his death by Jean Baptiste Beaubien

John Kinzie's house described from inside it: a long log cabin with a rude piazza, fronting the river directly opposite the fort, with a window that had a sight-line to the fort at night — the piazza confirmed again nine years later

a complete building count for the whole of the present Cook County in 1818: the fort's group, the Factor House, the Fur Company storehouse, Hardscrabble, Ouilmette's cabin and Kinzie's house, and nothing else

the river mouth's history — its natural outlet at the fort, its southward migration behind a sand spit driven by north-east winds, its position at The Pines a mile south as late as 1827, the soldiers' cut of spring 1828 and the sand's refilling of it

landscape: the prairie seen from Douglas Grove, the Blue Island grove and the Desplaines timber, wild onion and leek along the river, wild rice and head-high grass at Mud Lake, the old cultivated field on the River Guarie still legible as cornhills, and prairie fires dangerous enough to sink boats against

Hubbard's Trail, dated by the man who cut it (1822 to Danville, extended north to Chicago in 1824) and the State road from Vincennes to Chicago ordered in the winter of 1833-34 that adopted most of it
the settlement's size taken sideways: about forty men and women turned out to fight the fort fire in 1827, and a majority of the men at the fort that summer were Hubbard's own employees

for 1835, at one remove through McIlvaine: the brig Illinois lightered ashore on 25 May because the harbour could not take her, the passengers going on to the Green Tree Tavern, the Chicago American of 10 October 1835 on Hubbard's fire engine, and the March 1835 purchase of the eighty acres of Russell & Mather's addition for $5,000
one period document, and it is graded separately: Hubbard's letter to his sister headed 'Chicago, July 25, 1827', at data/sources/hubbard_letter_1827_07_25.json
what_it_does_not_supply: Hubbard's own eyewitness on 1835. HIS NARRATIVE ENDS IN NOVEMBER 1830 and the closing note says so in as many words; the book's 1835 is Caroline McIlvaine's, written in 1911

any plat position, lot, or measured coordinate. Every placement here is prose — 'west and a little south of the fort', 'about where Wells street now crosses the river' — and several are given in streets that did not exist when the thing described did
reliable dimensions. 'A square of about six hundred feet' for the Fort Dearborn stockade is a pace-estimate at sixty years' distance and is much larger than the fort this project reconstructs

a consistent account of the officers' quarters: page 36 puts them outside the pickets and built of hewn logs, page 167 puts the commanding officers' former quarters in a brick building just within the north stockade and the log quarters within the pickets on the west. The book contradicts itself and this project does not resolve it
the right year for the Pottawatomie payment and the fort fire: page 167 prints 1828 where the section heading, the surrounding narrative and Hubbard's own dated letter all say July 1827
the names of the officers commanding Fort Dearborn after 19 June 1833 — Hubbard says he could not find them in the War Department records, so the source names nobody in command during the scene year
a residence for anybody in 1835. Every person Hubbard names, he names for what they did between 1812 and 1830
page images. This reading is of the Internet Archive's OCR text of the scan, corroborated against the deposited PDF's own text layer; no claim here is scan_verified

citations.citation: Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-98, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)
transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.

what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.
what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.

citations.citation: Whistler, Captain John. "Fort Dearborn" [draught of the garrison and its vicinity], dated in the parade 'January 25th 1808', with its 'Index annexed to the Draught of Fort Dearborn &c.' signed at Fort Dearborn 20 February 1808. Original in the files of the War Department, Washington. Reproduced as the plate 'Fort Dearborn and Vicinity in 1808. From the original draft by Captain Whistler in the archives of the War Department at Washington', facing p. 164 of Quaife, Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835 (Chicago, 1913); the index is printed in full in note 413 on the same pages.
what_it_supplies: the first fort's garrison in plan at a stated scale: the double row of pickets, the two blockhouses at the north-west and south-east angles, the four barracks ranges, the magazine, two small houses, the main gate, the parade and the flagstaff
the drafter's index of 34 numbered features, and the note that two of them (the covered way and the gutters) are omitted from their places
the arrangement of the factor's and agent's establishments, stables, gardens and the houses across the river, by position only and not to scale
what_it_does_not_supply: any building height: the folded elevations disagree with each other
the fort's bearing to true north: no north arrow was found on the reproduction
the covered way to the river and the gutters, which the index itself says are omitted
anything about the second fort of 1816

research_note: ANTOINE OUILMETTE'S HOUSE (T-2486), the third no. 31 house on Whistler's draught of January 1808, the one nearest the Kinzie house. IN AUGUST 1812 it is the one house in Chicago whose household did not leave: Currey has the family stay because 'Ouilmette was regarded by the Potawatamis as belonging to their tribe'; Wau-Bun ch. XIX has Black Partridge bring Mrs. Helm here in a Frenchwoman's dress on the 16th, Mrs. Bisson hide her under the edge of a feather bed and sit sewing before it while the search went through the room, and a sergeant the next afternoon 'steal cautiously into the garden of Ouilmette, where he concealed himself for a time behind some currant-bushes' and climb 'through a small back window into the room where the family were'. The garden and its currants stand behind the house as ouilmette_garden_1812 in data/flora (a planting). NOT BUILT: the small back window, because the log_dwelling archetype pierces no back wall; a kit change, not a reading, would add it. NO PICTURE SHOWS IT, so it carries no image gate. Eastman's view of 1820 is the one picture of the north bank near its date, and through its solved camera (data/reference_views/kinzie_house_1812/eastman_1820.json) this house falls at x 1644-1690 px, off the engraving, whose right edge is at about x 1601. Three retrospective pictures take its seat inside their frames and draw trees or open ground there: Cram's 1893 engraving of the mansion (x 271-340 px, at the picture's left edge, trees), the Teich postcard painting (x 12-98, trees and the road) and Gemmell's bird's-eye lithograph (x 1213-1237, open prairie); none is a sighting of 1812, the first two show the place in the 1830s and later, and none names this house. PETTELL'S CABIN, which Currey puts 'near the Kinzie house', is not built beside it: data/exclusions.json pettell_cabin_1812 gives the ruling. It carries review_required and touches_removal: it reconstructs a Métis household's house at Chicago, the household that sheltered people on the day after the battle, and its Potawatomi family's later reservation on the north shore is part of the removal history this project is careful with (AGENTS.md § Standing constraint). Nobody is drawn in or near it.
